content: Red birthmarks are skin markings caused by blood vessels that develop either before or shortly after birth. These vascular birthmarks are characterized by their red appearance due to the presence of blood vessels near the skin's surface. Symptoms of Red Birthmarks: These birthmarks often resemble blood vessels or appear as red skin lesions. The appearance and location of red birthmarks vary depending on the type: Cavernous hemangiomas: These present as red-blue, spongy masses of tissue filled with blood. Port-wine stains: These are flat, red or purple marks, most commonly found on the face. Their size can range from very small to covering over half of the body surface. Salmon patches: These are small, pink, flat spots caused by visible capillaries under the skin. They are most commonly found on the forehead, eyelids, upper lip, between the eyebrows, or on the back of the neck. These patches may become more noticeable when the infant cries or during temperature changes. Strawberry hemangiomas: These are made up of small, closely packed blood vessels and can appear anywhere on the body, though they are most common on the neck and face. Causes of Red Birthmarks: Red birthmarks are vascular in nature, meaning they are composed of blood vessels close to the skin's surface. The exact cause of hemangiomas, a common type of vascular birthmark, is unknown. Their red color is due to the development of blood vessels at the site. Strawberry hemangiomas: These may develop several weeks after birth and are also known as nevus vascularis, capillary hemangioma, or hemangioma simplex. Cavernous hemangiomas: These are similar to strawberry hemangiomas but are located deeper in the skin. Salmon patches: Also called stork bites, these are extremely common and occur in 30-50% of newborns. Port-wine stains: These are flat hemangiomas made of dilated blood capillaries. When located on the face, they may be associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome. Diagnosis: All birthmarks should be examined by a healthcare provider to determine their type and any potential complications. Diagnosis is primarily based on the appearance of the skin lesion. However, deeper birthmarks may require additional tests such as: Biopsy CT scan MRI When to Seek Medical Care: It is important to have all birthmarks evaluated by a healthcare provider to assess the need for treatment, identify possible complications, and determine the prognosis. Treatment Options: Many types of red birthmarks, such as strawberry hemangiomas, cavernous hemangiomas, and salmon patches, are temporary and do not require treatment. Nevus flammeus (a type of hemangioma) may not need treatment unless it is disfiguring, causes psychological distress, is painful, or changes in appearance. Permanent birthmarks are typically not treated unless they cause symptoms or until the child reaches school age. However, port-wine stains on the face are an exception and should be treated early with a yellow pulsed-dye laser to prevent psychological and social issues. Treatment options include: Concealing cosmetics (e.g., Covermark) to hide permanent birthmarks. Cortisone (oral or injected) to reduce the size of rapidly growing hemangiomas that obstruct vision or vital organs. Cryotherapy (freezing), laser surgery, or surgical removal for certain cases. Prognosis: Most birthmarks do not cause problems beyond cosmetic concerns. Many birthmarks resolve on their own by the time a child reaches school age, though some are permanent: Strawberry hemangiomas: These typically grow quickly, stabilize, and then regress. About 95% disappear by the age of 9, though slight discoloration or puckering of the skin may remain. Cavernous hemangiomas: These often resolve on their own as the child approaches school age. Port-wine stains: These are usually permanent. Salmon patches: These often fade as the child grows, though patches on the back of the neck may persist but are usually hidden by hair. Possible Complications: Emotional distress due to the appearance of the birthmark. Occasional discomfort or bleeding from vascular birthmarks. Scarring or complications following surgical removal. Prevention: There is no known way to prevent the development of birthmarks.
